title: The Conveyancer's Chambers: Arthur Cayley, Matrices, and the Sadleirian Chair
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Richmond, Surrey: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested, 16 August 1821, MacTutor and Britannica agreeing. No source consulted names the house, so the coordinate marks the town and not a building.
stops.campa: Henry Cayley trades out of St Petersburg and happens to be home in England when his wife, Maria Antonia Doughty, is delivered of a son at Richmond in Surrey on the sixteenth of August. The boy is English by an accident of the calendar. In the household he is going back to, the servants speak Russian, the counting house speaks English, and the drawing room speaks French. The house he is born in goes unrecorded; the town is the whole of what the register keeps. Within weeks the family carries him back east.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Arthur Cayley'
suggested_refs: Parish registers of Richmond, Surrey, for August 1821

stops.name: St Petersburg: the counting house
stops.date_confidence: the childhood residence 1821-1828 is attested in MacTutor; the date here is an ordering placeholder within it. No address survives in anything consulted, so the coordinate marks the city centre only.
stops.campa: For seven years the boy grows up in the expatriate merchant quarter of the Russian capital, in three languages at once, none of which he will later be famous for. His father sells and ships. His mother is English, though the commemorative literature written after his death will insist she was Russian and explain her son by it. Nothing of the address survives, and no anecdote of these years reaches the biographers except the fact of the languages. Whether he kept any Russian into adulthood, nothing consulted says.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
suggested_refs: Records of the British merchant community at St Petersburg in the 1820s
Jemma Lorenat's metabiographical study of the Cayley 'Russian mother' legend, via Tony Crilly (not directly consulted: Springer login wall)

stops.name: 29 York Terrace, Regent's Park: the family comes home
stops.date_confidence: contradiction printed, not resolved. MacTutor gives the permanent return as 1828; Wikipedia, the 1911 Britannica ('left business in 1829'), Salmon (1883) and Macfarlane give 1829. The file takes the earlier date and leaves the later standing.
stops.campa: Henry Cayley leaves the Russian trade and brings the household back to London for good, taking a house on York Terrace at the edge of Regent's Park and a directorship of the London Assurance Corporation. The boy is seven, or eight. From here the geography of his life narrows to three addresses: an inn of court in London, a college in Cambridge, and a house at the bottom of a Cambridge lane. On the year of the return the sources will not agree. MacTutor gives 1828; Wikipedia, the 1911 Britannica, Salmon and Macfarlane give 1829.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley

stops.name: Blackheath: the private school
stops.date_confidence: the Blackheath schooling is attested but undated in the sources consulted; 1830 is an ordering placeholder between the family's return and the 1835 entry to King's College School. The first research pass conflated this school with the family's residence, which was at Regent's Park.
stops.campa: He is sent across the river to a private school at Blackheath, whose name nobody thought to write down. What gets written down is what the masters notice: the boy computes. Long numerical work that other children find punishing he treats as an amusement, and does at speed, for pleasure. The facility is conspicuous before he is ten. Blackheath lies on the Kent side of the Thames, well south of the family's house at Regent's Park; whether he boarded there or travelled, no source consulted says. Of the masters, of his schoolfellows, of the building itself, nothing else survives.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Arthur Cayley'
suggested_refs: The private schools of Blackheath village in the 1830s

stops.name: King's College School, the Strand: admitted early
stops.date_confidence: the year 1835 and the age of fourteen are attested in MacTutor. The term is not given, so the date defaults to January. A chemistry prize asserted in the first research pass, sourced there to the Wikipedia article on Cayley, is not in that article and has been dropped.
stops.campa: At fourteen, below the ordinary entrance age, he is admitted to the senior department of King's College School, which at that date occupies the basement of King's College London on the Strand. He takes prizes across several subjects. The college above him is six years old, the school inside it younger still, and the arrangement is literally subterranean: a boys' school in the cellars of a university, on the north bank, between Somerset House and the Inns of Court. He will spend most of his working life inside that half mile.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge: matriculation at seventeen
stops.date_confidence: the year and the age are attested in MacTutor; October is the Michaelmas term convention, not a documented day. The coordinate is the canonical Trinity pin already in use in the corpus, inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: He comes up to Trinity at seventeen. His first-year tutor is George Peacock, who twenty-five years earlier had founded the Analytical Society with Charles Babbage to drive Newton's dot notation out of Cambridge and put Leibniz's in its place, a campaign the undergraduates called the war of the d's against the dots. Peacock won it. Cayley arrives into the syllabus that victory built, and William Hopkins, the great private coach, pushes him further out still, into the continental mathematics the Tripos does not examine.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
working/journeys/charles_babbage.journey.json, for Peacock and Babbage as founders of the Analytical Society in 1813
suggested_refs: The Cambridge Analytical Society and the 1816 Lacroix translation of Peacock, Babbage and Herschel

stops.name: Cambridge Senate House: Senior Wrangler
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested in MacTutor. The Tripos was examined and the order posted in January; the day is not given in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: The Mathematical Tripos is examined by written paper over several January days and ranked to the last man, and the Senate House posts the order. Cayley is placed first: Senior Wrangler of his year, and first Smith's Prizeman on top of it. He is twenty. Forsyth will later record that Cayley denied the tripos story told about him by Bristed, whatever it was, as quite apocryphal; the denial survives and the story does not. What the rank buys him is a fellowship, four years of funding, and the right to publish as fast as he can write.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
A. R. Forsyth, 'Biographical Notice of Arthur Cayley', Collected Mathematical Papers vol. VIII, p. x
suggested_refs: The Cambridge Tripos order of merit for 1842

stops.name: Aberfeldy: the reading party
stops.date_confidence: summer 1842 is attested in MacTutor; July is a placeholder inside that season, not a documented month. Galton's recollection of Cayley's physique is a later memoir, not a contemporary record.
stops.campa: With the examinations behind him he goes north with Edmund Venables to lead a student reading party at Aberfeldy, in Perthshire, on the Tay. Among the students is Francis Galton, who remembers afterwards how slight the man was, and how little the body suggested what was in it. The party reads mathematics through a Highland summer. Venables writes to Stokes a joke about Cayley refusing to climb Schiehallion and repeat Maskelyne's weighing of the earth.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
suggested_refs: Edmund Venables's letter to G. G. Stokes on the Aberfeldy reading party
Francis Galton's recollections of Cayley

stops.name: Trinity College: the fellowship and the twenty-eight papers
stops.date_confidence: the fellowship election in 1842 and the roughly four further years at Cambridge are attested in MacTutor; October is a convention, not a documented day. The count of about 28 papers in the Cambridge Mathematical Journal is MacTutor's figure.
stops.campa: Elected Fellow of Trinity in the same year as the wranglership, he stays on about four years with no duty but to work. He had already published as an undergraduate in the Cambridge Mathematical Journal, which Duncan Farquharson Gregory edits; now he puts some twenty-eight papers into it. In 1843 comes On a Theory of Determinants, extending the machinery he will spend the next fifty years generalizing. In 1844 he begins writing to George Boole. Then the four years run out.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
suggested_refs: The Cambridge Mathematical Journal under D. F. Gregory, 1841-1845
Cayley, 'On a Theory of Determinants' (1843)

segments.name: The Alps, the Cathedral, and the Inn

stops.name: Chamonix and the Swiss Alps: the continental journey
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The 1844 journey with Venables through Switzerland and Italy comes to this file through the research pool, which attributes it to MacTutor and Crilly but could not re-fetch it independently. No source names any town or route, so Chamonix is the compiler's placeholder for the standard British Alpine gateway of the period and is not an attested stop; the Italian leg is described here rather than given a pin of its own, for the same reason.
stops.campa: He travels with Edmund Venables through the Swiss Alps and on into Italy. No letter, no diary, no named town survives from the trip, only the fact of it, and the standing knowledge that travel, architecture and painting are the pleasures he keeps outside mathematics all his life. He paints in watercolour. He will go on looking at buildings the way he looks at forms, which is to say for their structure, and Italy is where England's educated men go to do that. He is twenty-two.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley (via the research pool; the specific trip was not independently re-fetched)
suggested_refs: Tony Crilly, Arthur Cayley: Mathematician Laureate of the Victorian Age (2006), on the continental journeys

stops.name: Lincoln Cathedral: the letter to George Boole
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. A surviving letter to Boole expresses the wish to visit him at Lincoln and see the cathedral; no source consulted confirms the visit ever happened. The stop records an intention, not an attested arrival, and the date is an ordering placeholder in the correspondence, which began in 1844.
stops.campa: He has been corresponding with George Boole for a year, a schoolmaster in Lincoln with no university behind him and an algebra of his own coming. In one surviving letter Cayley says he would like to come to Lincoln, see Boole, and see the cathedral on its hill. Whether he ever went, nothing consulted says. The same year he publishes two papers on linear transformations and algebraic forms that lay the ground of invariant theory, the subject he and James Joseph Sylvester will spend three decades building between them.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
suggested_refs: The Cayley-Boole correspondence, begun 1844
Cayley's two 1845 papers on linear transformations and algebraic forms

stops.name: Lincoln's Inn: admitted
stops.date_confidence: attested, 20 April 1846, Britannica and the Wilberforce Chambers article agreeing. The coordinate corrects the research pool's 51.5155, -0.1116, which sat about 250 m south-west of the Inn.
stops.campa: On the twentieth of April he is admitted to Lincoln's Inn. He is twenty-four, a Fellow of Trinity with a wranglership and a shelf of published papers behind him, and he is entering the law because the law pays and pure mathematics in England does not. Chancery is the branch he chooses: trusts, settlements, the conveyance of land, the most paper-bound and least eloquent corner of the profession. For the next seventeen years his working address in term time is a set of chambers off Chancery Lane.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Arthur Cayley'
E. Campbell, 'Chancery barrister and mathematician: Arthur Cayley (1821-1895)', Wilberforce Chambers
Wikipedia, 'Lincoln's Inn'
suggested_refs: The admissions registers of the Honourable Society of Lincoln's Inn, April 1846

stops.name: 2 Stone Buildings, Lincoln's Inn: the pupil of Christie
stops.date_confidence: the pupillage under Jonathan Henry Christie at 2 Stone Buildings is attested in the Wilberforce Chambers article; the month is a placeholder after the April admission. The coordinate places Stone Buildings at the Robert Taylor range of 1775-1780 in the north-east corner of the Inn, correcting the pool's 51.5158, -0.1122. The anecdote quoted below reaches print through a memoir of the profession, not a contemporary record.
stops.campa: He walks into the chambers of Jonathan Henry Christie, the leading conveyancer of the day, sends in his card, and asks to be taken as a pupil. He has no letter of introduction and volunteers nothing. Christie has to extract the man's history a question at a time. Installed, he writes mathematics in the same room and the same hours as the law, two to three hundred papers across the legal years, and drafts settlements for the Marquis of Bute and for the Earl of Shrewsbury's Staffordshire estates.
stops.quote: Mr Cayley arrived at Stone Buildings, sent in his card, was admitted, and asked to be taken as a pupil. Christie inquired whether he had any introduction; the reply was, No. Had he been at a University? Yes. Christie, who seldom had a vacant chair in his pupil room, used to describe himself as not having been very favourably inclined towards this monosyllabic applicant. However, he had been at the University and it might be worth while to inquire further. Christie did so, and by successive and separate questions elicited the information that Cayley's University was Cambridge; his college Trinity; that he had taken a degree; in honours; in mathematical honours; that he had been a Wrangler; that he had been Senior Wrangler.
stops.quote_source: M. G. Davidson, in John Savill Vaizey, The Institute, A Club of Conveyancing Counsel: Memoirs of Former Members (1895-1907), reproduced in E. Campbell, 'Chancery barrister and mathematician: Arthur Cayley (1821-1895)', Wilberforce Chambers
sources: E. Campbell, 'Chancery barrister and mathematician: Arthur Cayley (1821-1895)', Wilberforce Chambers (PDF fetched at HTTP 200; the HTML page returns 403)
suggested_refs: 2 Stone Buildings, Lincoln's Inn, chambers of Jonathan Henry Christie
Davidson's Precedents and Forms in Conveyancing, 3rd ed. (1873), vol. III Part II, p. 1067, and Forsyth's footnote on it

stops.name: Trinity College Dublin: Hamilton on quaternions
stops.date_confidence: attested as June 1848 in the Wilberforce Chambers article; the venue is confirmed by Wikipedia's article on Hamilton, which records that the Lectures on Quaternions were delivered from 1848 onward in the halls of Trinity College, Dublin. The day is not given. The first research pass tagged this a reconstruction for want of a date; the hedge is withdrawn. George Salmon's presence, asserted in that first pass, could not be confirmed and no one but Hamilton and Cayley is staged here.
stops.campa: In June, still a pupil in Christie's chambers, he crosses to Dublin to hear William Rowan Hamilton lecture on quaternions in the halls of Trinity College. Hamilton had cut i, j and k into a bridge over the Royal Canal five years before, and now holds that he has found the algebra of three-dimensional space itself, and under it a deeper truth: that algebra is the science of pure time. Cayley likes the man and keeps up with him. The metaphysics he never accepts, and thirty-five years later he says so from a president's chair at Southport.
stops.quote: I cannot myself recognize the connection of algebra with the notion of time; granting that the notion of continuous progression presents itself and is of importance, I do not see that it is in anywise the fundamental notion of the science. And still less can I appreciate the manner in which the author connects with the notion of time his algebraical couple, or imaginary magnitude, a + b sqrt(-1).
stops.quote_source: Arthur Cayley, presidential address to the British Association for the Advancement of Science, Southport, 1883, on Hamilton's 'algebra as the science of pure time', quoted in Alexander Macfarlane, Lectures on Ten British Mathematicians of the Nineteenth Century (1916), ch. 5. Spoken thirty-five years after the Dublin lectures; the radical sign is rendered here as sqrt for plain text.
sources: E. Campbell, 'Chancery barrister and mathematician: Arthur Cayley (1821-1895)', Wilberforce Chambers
Wikipedia, 'William Rowan Hamilton'
Alexander Macfarlane, Lectures on Ten British Mathematicians of the Nineteenth Century (1916), ch. 5
suggested_refs: Hamilton's Lectures on Quaternions (1853), grown out of the courses begun in 1848

stops.name: Lincoln's Inn: called to the Bar
stops.date_confidence: attested, 3 May 1849, in MacTutor and confirmed by the Wilberforce Chambers article, which also confirms the figure of between two and three hundred papers published in the period 1849 to 1863.
stops.campa: On the third of May he is called to the Bar and begins fourteen years of practice. The fellow-pupils know he was Senior Wrangler and cannot get him to mention it. He is agreeable, unworldly, amused by the badinage of the pupil room as though jokes were a new invention, and grinds through conveyancing work that a colleague suspects he does not much enjoy. He is good at it. Davidson's Precedents prints one of his settlements with a footnote calling attention to the remarkable skill in it.
stops.quote: We fellow-pupils knew that Arthur Cayley had been the Senior Wrangler of his year, and that he possessed extraordinary abilities; but they were not indicated by his personal bearing, and the retiring modesty of his disposition prevented him from ever alluding to the honours he had won at Cambridge. He had one of the most unsophisticated minds I have ever known; jokes, and the badinage of the pupil-room, seemed to be delightful novelties to him, and his face beamed with amusement as he listened to them without taking much part in the conversation, being content to devote his time assiduously to work which I suspect was not altogether congenial to his taste...
stops.quote_source: T. C. Wright, fellow pupil in Christie's chambers, quoted in A. R. Forsyth, 'Biographical Notice of Arthur Cayley', The Collected Mathematical Papers of Arthur Cayley, vol. VIII (Cambridge University Press, 1895), p. xiv; reprinted in E. Campbell's Wilberforce Chambers article
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
E. Campbell, 'Chancery barrister and mathematician: Arthur Cayley (1821-1895)', Wilberforce Chambers
A. R. Forsyth, Collected Mathematical Papers vol. VIII, p. xiv
suggested_refs: Davidson's Precedents and Forms in Conveyancing, 3rd ed. (1873), vol. III Part II, p. 1067

stops.name: Somerset House: elected Fellow of the Royal Society
stops.date_confidence: attested, 3 June 1852, in the Royal Society's Making Science catalogue record. The research pool's verifier did not pull the primary election record itself. The coordinate corrects the pool's 51.5109, -0.1246, which fell about 470 m west near Charing Cross; the Society occupied the east wing of Somerset House from 1780.
stops.campa: On the third of June the Royal Society, then in the east wing of Somerset House on the Strand, elects him a Fellow. He is thirty, a working barrister, and the papers that earn the election were written in the intervals of drafting other men's trusts. His chambers stand half a mile north-east; the basement school where he learned is in the next building along the Strand. The Royal Medal follows in 1859 and the Copley in 1882. He holds no university post until 1863.

stops.name: 2 Stone Buildings: theta to the n equals one
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested in MacTutor; no month is given, so the date defaults to January. The pin is his chambers, where he was working, not a publication venue.
stops.campa: He publishes a paper on the theory of groups as depending on the symbolic equation theta^n = 1, and in it he does something nobody has quite done: he treats a group as a set of symbols with a law of combination, cut loose from the permutations and substitutions that had always carried it. He gives a multiplication table. It is now taken as the point where abstract group theory begins. He writes it in a conveyancer's chambers off Chancery Lane, and for twenty years almost nobody reads it.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
suggested_refs: Cayley, 'On the theory of groups, as depending on the symbolic equation theta^n = 1' (1854)

stops.name: Marischal College, Aberdeen: the chair not got
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as a physical stop. MacTutor records the unsuccessful candidacy for the chair of natural philosophy in 1856, but no source consulted says whether Cayley travelled to Aberdeen or applied by correspondence. The month is not given.
stops.campa: He is a candidate for the chair of natural philosophy at Marischal College and does not get it. Whether he went north to be looked at or applied by letter, the record does not say. Three years later he will show interest in the Glasgow chair of astronomy and not get that either. The later accounts have him nobly choosing the Bar over an academic salary; both applications fall in the middle of the Bar years. What he wanted from a Scottish chair of natural philosophy, no source consulted explains.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
suggested_refs: The 1856 election to the chair of natural philosophy, Marischal College, Aberdeen

stops.name: 2 Stone Buildings: A Memoir on the Theory of Matrices
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested in MacTutor and Britannica; the Philosophical Transactions issue is 1858 and no day applies. The 1855 sketch of matrix multiplication, written in French for a German periodical, is folded into this stop rather than pinned separately, since both were written in the same chambers.
stops.campa: Three years earlier, writing in French for a German journal, he had sketched a rule for what he called compounding two arrays of numbers. Now he gives the Philosophical Transactions the full statement: a rectangle of numbers is an object in its own right, with an addition, a multiplication that does not commute, an inverse, and an algebra. He proves that a matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation for the two-by-two case, illustrates the three-by-three, and states the general principle without proving it. Someone else will supply the proof.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Arthur Cayley'
suggested_refs: Cayley, 'A Memoir on the Theory of Matrices', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society (1858)
Cayley's 1855 introductory note on 'compounding', published in French in a German periodical

stops.name: 2 Stone Buildings: the Sixth Memoir upon Quantics
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; no month applies to the memoir. Klein's reinterpretation dates from 1871, within Cayley's lifetime, and is stated here as the later reading it was, not as anything Cayley intended.
stops.campa: In the sixth of his memoirs on quantics he defines distance projectively, by a conic he calls the absolute, and writes that descriptive geometry is all geometry. He means projective geometry swallowing the metric one. Twelve years later Felix Klein reads the memoir as something Cayley did not intend and could not have used: a working model of non-Euclidean geometry, with the absolute doing the work of curvature. The construction goes into the world under both their names.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
research pool account of the Cayley-Klein projective metric
suggested_refs: Cayley, 'A Sixth Memoir upon Quantics' (1859)
Felix Klein's 1871 papers on non-Euclidean geometry and the Cayley absolute

stops.name: Cambridge: elected the first Sadleirian Professor
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested in Britannica and MacTutor; the month of election is not given in the sources consulted, so the date defaults to January. The aphorism quoted below is quoted only as the thing Cayley denied; it is not his.
stops.campa: Cambridge founds a chair of pure mathematics out of the Lady Sadleir bequest and elects him to it, the first man to hold it. He gives up the practice. The salary is a fraction of what Chancery paid him and he takes it without visible hesitation, which is the sort of act that attracts apocrypha. Within his own lifetime he is being quoted as having said that law exists to say a thing in the greatest number of words and mathematics in the fewest. He repudiated the remark, and the possibility of ever having held the view.
stops.quote: It may be added that Cayley declared the story about him in the tripos, recorded by Bristed, to be quite apocryphal. So also was another story, belonging to a later part of his life, according to which he is reported to have said that 'the object of law was to say a thing in the greatest number of words, and of mathematics to say it in the fewest': this view, and the possibility of his ever having held it, he repudiated entirely.
stops.quote_source: A. R. Forsyth, 'Biographical Notice of Arthur Cayley', The Collected Mathematical Papers of Arthur Cayley, vol. VIII (Cambridge University Press, 1895), footnote on p. x. Forsyth is debunking the aphorism, not reporting it: the words inside the inner quotation marks are a rumour Cayley denied and must never be printed as his own.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Arthur Cayley'
MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
A. R. Forsyth, Collected Mathematical Papers vol. VIII, p. x
suggested_refs: The Lady Sadleir bequest and the 1863 foundation of the Sadleirian Professorship of Pure Mathematics

stops.name: Lewisham: the marriage to Susan Moline
stops.date_confidence: attested, 8 September 1863, in MacTutor and the Mill Road Cemetery project. The parish church is not named in anything consulted. The coordinate corrects the pool's 51.4452, -0.0208, which fell about 2.1 km south-west in the Rushey Green area.
stops.campa: On the eighth of September, in the same year he changes profession, he marries Susan Moline, daughter of a manager of the London and County Bank. He is forty-two. Lewisham is still a Kentish parish on the outer edge of London, and the church they marry in is not named in anything consulted. They will have a son and a daughter, and Susan will outlive him in the house they are about to buy in Cambridge, keeping it with their daughter Mary after his death. Of the marriage itself the record holds almost nothing, which is true of nearly all his private life.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
Mill Road Cemetery project, 'Arthur Cayley'

stops.name: Cambridge: the inaugural lecture
stops.date_confidence: contradiction printed, not resolved. MacTutor gives 8 November 1863, and this file follows it because MacTutor was the source actually fetched. Tony Crilly's specialist study of the unpublished lecture text gives 3 November 1863; that article (Springer, doi 10.1007/s00283-023-10278-2) is behind a login wall and could not be read. The lecture room within Cambridge is not specified anywhere consulted, so the coordinate is a town-centre placeholder.
stops.campa: He delivers his inaugural lecture as Sadleirian Professor under the title Analytical geometry: Introductory lecture. The room is not recorded, and the text was never published; it survives in manuscript and has been studied once, by a specialist, who dates the delivery five days earlier than the standard reference does. The professorship, by its terms, obliges him to explain the principles of pure mathematics and to further their advancement. He holds it for thirty-two years.
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Arthur Cayley
Tony Crilly, on the unpublished inaugural lecture, The Mathematical Intelligencer (not read: login wall)

stops.name: Garden House, Little St Mary's Lane: the house at the bottom of the lane
stops.date_confidence: the 1864 purchase is reported by the Mill Road Cemetery project, which the research pool did not independently re-fetch in its verification pass. No month is given.
stops.campa: He buys Garden House, at the bottom of Little St Mary's Lane where it runs out onto Coe Fen and the river meadows, five minutes from the colleges and facing open grass. The house stands at the southern edge of the town, past the last of the college backs, where Cambridge stops being a university and becomes a fen. It is his address for the last thirty-one years of his life and the address on nearly everything he writes. Susan runs it, the children grow up in it, the papers accumulate in it. He dies in it.
sources: Mill Road Cemetery project, 'Arthur Cayley'
suggested_refs: Garden House, Little St Mary's Lane, Cambridge, by Coe Fen

stops.name: University College London: president of the London Mathematical Society
stops.date_confidence: the presidency 1868-1870 is reported in the research pool and is consistent with the standard LMS presidents list; the pool did not re-fetch it in verification. The Society was founded in 1865 and met initially at University College London, but the venue during his own presidency is not itemized anywhere consulted, so the coordinate is the Society's historic meeting home rather than a documented room.
stops.campa: The London Mathematical Society is three years old, founded by a son of De Morgan and meeting at University College in Gower Street, when it elects Cayley its president. The society exists because English mathematicians had nowhere to read papers to each other outside the Royal Society, which was not primarily theirs, and which had made him a Fellow sixteen years earlier. He has been publishing at industrial rate since he was twenty and is five years into the Sadleirian chair. He serves from 1868 to 1870.
sources: London Mathematical Society timeline (lms.ac.uk/history/london-mathematical-society-timeline)
research pool account of the 1868 presidency

stops.name: Burlington House: president of the Royal Astronomical Society
stops.date_confidence: the presidency 1872-1874 is on the RAS past-presidents list, which the research pool cited but did not re-fetch in verification. The honorary Trinity fellowship of 1872 is attested in Britannica; the ordinary fellowship of 1875 is carried from Britannica as a reconstruction.
stops.campa: He takes the chair of the Royal Astronomical Society at Burlington House for two years. He is not an observer and never was. What he brings to astronomy is the analytical machinery: the perturbation work, the lunar theory arithmetic that a century of British astronomers had been grinding out by hand. He is fifty-one, and he spent his thirties drafting settlements. The same year Trinity makes him an honorary Fellow, restoring in title what the statutes had taken from him thirty years before.

stops.name: Girton College: teaching in the earliest days
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia attests that in the early days of Girton College Cayley gave direct help in teaching, but does not date it. October 1873 is the college's move from Benslow House, Hitchin, to the Girton site; any teaching in the very earliest days may therefore have happened at Hitchin, in Hertfordshire, and not here. The coordinate corrects the pool's 52.2222, 0.0847, about 715 m south. Charlotte Angas Scott was at Girton, not at Newnham, as the first research pass had it.
stops.campa: The women's college that opened at Hitchin in 1869 moves to a new building at Girton, two miles out of Cambridge on the road north, and Cayley gives direct help in the teaching. Cambridge will not grant these students degrees for another seventy-five years. In 1876 Charlotte Angas Scott enters; in 1880 she sits the Tripos; then she stays on to research algebraic geometry under his supervision, attending his lectures on modern algebra, Abelian functions, the theory of numbers, substitutions and seminvariants.

stops.name: Trinity College: the portrait fund
stops.date_confidence: the 1874 Dickinson portrait and the 1884 Longmaid portrait, both in Trinity's collection, are attested in Wikipedia. The first research pass credited MacTutor, which mentions neither, and called Maxwell's contribution a poem; Wikipedia calls it an address praising Cayley's principal works. The verse itself is real and is reprinted by Macfarlane and by Forsyth, and is quoted here as verse without asserting the occasion's genre.
stops.campa: Friends raise a subscription and commission Lowes Cato Dickinson to paint him for the college, which had elected him a Fellow at twenty-one and then could not keep him. James Clerk Maxwell sends the committee lines in praise of the sitter's principal works, which is not the usual currency of a portrait fund: determinants, the cubic surface with its twenty-seven lines, and space of n dimensions each get a stanza. Ten years later William Longmaid paints him again. Both canvases hang at Trinity.
stops.quote: O wretched race of men, to space confined! What honour can ye pay to him whose mind To that which lies beyond hath penetrated? The symbols he hath formed shall sound his praise, And lead him on through unimagined ways To conquests new, in worlds not yet created.
stops.quote_source: James Clerk Maxwell, 'To the Committee of the Cayley Portrait Fund' (1874), first stanza, reproduced in Alexander Macfarlane, Lectures on Ten British Mathematicians of the Nineteenth Century (1916), ch. 5

stops.name: Newnham College: chairman of the council
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia attests that for some years Cayley was chairman of the council of Newnham College, and gives no dates at either end; 1875 is an ordering placeholder only. The coordinate corrects the pool's 52.1958, 0.1080, about 410 m off. Charlotte Angas Scott does not belong to this stop and has been moved to Girton.
stops.campa: He chairs the council of Newnham College for some years, the second of the Cambridge foundations for women, on the same side of the same argument he had joined at Girton. The two colleges sit on opposite edges of the town, Girton two miles north on its own land, Newnham just west across the mill pond from his own house, so that for a stretch of the 1870s he is teaching at one and governing the other. No source consulted dates the chairmanship at either end, and the college's council minute books for the decade were not read.

stops.name: Cambridge University Press: An Elementary Treatise on Elliptic Functions
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested in MacTutor and Britannica; no month applies. The lineage from Gauss stated in the campa is disciplinary, not personal: no source claims any contact or correspondence between Cayley and Gauss, and none was found.
stops.campa: The Press publishes the one book of his that is not a collection of papers: a treatise on elliptic functions, the doubly periodic functions Carl Friedrich Gauss had worked out privately and never published, and that Abel and Jacobi then found again in the open. Cayley is not adding a new theory here. He is doing what he does with every subject he touches, laying it out as a system so that other people can walk into it. Cambridge undergraduates learn elliptic functions from this book for a generation. He never writes another.

stops.name: Garden House: On the Colourings of Maps
stops.date_confidence: the 1879 paper and its venue are attested in Wikipedia's article on the four colour theorem, which also records that Cayley credited the conjecture to De Morgan. MacTutor does not mention the four-colour problem at all, so the first research pass's attribution to it was wrong and has been replaced. No month applies. The pin is his house, where he was working, not the publication venue.
stops.campa: He publishes a short paper asking whether four colours suffice to distinguish the countries of any map, and he publishes it, of all places, in the Proceedings of the Royal Geographical Society. He does not claim the question. He credits it to De Morgan and says plainly that he cannot solve it. What the paper does is put the problem in front of mathematicians who had let it lapse, and there it stays, unproved, for another ninety-seven years. He is fifty-eight, and the note runs to a few pages.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Four color theorem'

stops.name: Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore: the American lectures
stops.date_confidence: January to May 1882 and the subject, Abelian and theta functions, are attested in MacTutor; Britannica attests the invitation. The first research pass credited the Wilberforce Chambers article, which says nothing about Johns Hopkins. The coordinate is approximate: Wikipedia gives no address or coordinates for the original downtown Baltimore campus, which the university left for Homewood in 1902. The lecture hall is not named anywhere consulted.
stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic in January and lectures at Johns Hopkins until May, on Abelian and theta functions. The university is six years old and its mathematics is James Joseph Sylvester's: Sylvester, his closest collaborator since 1847, the other architect of invariant theory, the man he had walked the squares of Lincoln's Inn with when both of them were lawyers who would rather have been something else. Sylvester had been brought to Baltimore in 1876 to build an American research school out of nothing. Cayley comes to see it standing.

stops.name: Burlington House: the Copley Medal
stops.date_confidence: Britannica and the Royal Society catalogue give 1882; some secondary sources print 1881, and that disagreement is left standing rather than argued. No month is given, so the date defaults to January, which places this stop alongside the Baltimore lectures of the same year rather than after them.
stops.campa: The Royal Society gives him the Copley, its oldest and highest award, thirty years after electing him and twenty-three after the Royal Medal. He is sixty-one. The work it covers is by now several hundred papers on invariants, matrices, groups, determinants, quantics, elliptic functions, the geometry of n dimensions and the perturbations of the moon, produced across a career in which he held no mathematical post at all until he was forty-two. Britannica and the Society's own catalogue date the award 1882. Some secondary accounts print 1881, and nothing consulted reconciles them.

stops.name: Southport: the presidential address
stops.date_confidence: the year and the Southport meeting are attested in Britannica and Wikipedia; the month of the address is not given in the sources consulted, so the date defaults to January and should not be read as the date of delivery. No hall within Southport is named anywhere consulted.
stops.campa: The British Association meets at Southport on the Lancashire coast and he presides. He talks about non-Euclidean geometry, about whether space is a fact or a form of thought, and about Hamilton's claim that algebra is the science of pure time, which he takes apart in front of the meeting thirty-five years after Dublin. The address is a survey of the progress of pure mathematics, given to an audience that has come expecting something it can follow. He opens by telling them he knows it.
stops.quote: I wish to speak to you to-night upon Mathematics. I am quite aware of the difficulty arising from the abstract nature of my subject; and if, as I fear, many or some of you, recalling the providential addresses at former meetings, should wish that you were now about to have from a different President a discourse on a different subject, I can very well sympathize with you in the feeling.
stops.quote_source: Arthur Cayley, opening of the presidential address 'The Progress of Pure Mathematics', British Association for the Advancement of Science, Southport, 1883, quoted in Alexander Macfarlane, Lectures on Ten British Mathematicians of the Nineteenth Century (1916), ch. 5

stops.name: University College London: the first De Morgan Medal
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested in MacTutor, Britannica and the LMS timeline; no ceremony venue is specified anywhere consulted, so the coordinate is the Society's historic meeting home at University College London rather than a documented room.
stops.campa: The London Mathematical Society strikes a medal in the name of its first president, Augustus De Morgan, and gives the first one to Cayley. He had been the society's president himself sixteen years earlier, and it was De Morgan's four-colour question that he had put back into circulation five years before. The society had been founded because there was nowhere else in England to read a mathematical paper aloud. He is sixty-three. After this one the medal goes out once every three years.

stops.name: Cambridge University Press: the Collected Papers begun
stops.date_confidence: attested in Britannica and Wikipedia: publication began in 1889, ran to thirteen quarto volumes and about 967 papers, and Forsyth completed the edition after Cayley's death. The archive.org copy of volume 1 carries the stated date 1889.
stops.campa: The Press begins printing his collected mathematical papers in quarto, and he undertakes to edit them himself. He is sixty-seven. The task means reading through half a century of his own work, some of it published in journals that no longer exist, and putting nine hundred and sixty-seven papers into an order. He gets through seven volumes. The finished set runs to thirteen and takes eight years, and the remaining six are the work of the man who succeeds him in the Sadleirian chair.

stops.name: Garden House: a theorem on trees
stops.date_confidence: the paper is attested; its bibliographic details (Quarterly Journal of Pure and Applied Mathematics 23, 376-378) come from the research pool and were not independently re-fetched. Borchardt's earlier 1860 enumeration by a different method is carried from the same pool. No month applies. The pin is the house he was working in.
stops.campa: In three pages of the Quarterly Journal of Pure and Applied Mathematics he counts something and does not make much of it. Carl Wilhelm Borchardt had reached the same count by another route in 1860, and Cayley says so in the paper. It is a footnote inside an output of nine hundred and sixty-seven papers, written at sixty-eight in the last decade of his life, and it is now the one result of his that most of the people who use it can name. What it says is this: the labelled trees on n points number n to the power n minus two.

stops.name: Garden House: coordinates versus quaternions
stops.date_confidence: the 1894 exchange in the Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh is attested and the quotation was verified twice by raw fetch against Macfarlane's reprint. The 1890 contribution of Chapter VI to the new edition of Tait's Elementary Treatise on Quaternions is carried from the research pool and was not independently re-fetched; it is folded into this stop rather than pinned separately.
stops.campa: Four years earlier he had written Chapter VI for a new edition of Tait's treatise on quaternions, which is a strange thing for a man who never accepted them to agree to do. Now, at seventy-two, he takes Tait on directly in the Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, and the argument he makes is not that quaternions are wrong. He says they are beautiful, more beautiful than anything they are used for, and that to use one you must first unfold it into coordinates. Hamilton has been dead for twenty-nine years.
stops.quote: I have the highest admiration for the notion of a quaternion; but, as I consider the full moon far more beautiful than any moonlit view, so I regard the notion of a quaternion as far more beautiful than any of its applications. As another illustration, I compare a quaternion formula to a pocket-map, a capital thing to put in one's pocket, but which for use must be unfolded: the formula, to be understood, must be translated into coordinates.
stops.quote_source: Arthur Cayley, 'Coordinates versus Quaternions', Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh (1894), quoted verbatim in Alexander Macfarlane, Lectures on Ten British Mathematicians of the Nineteenth Century (1916), ch. 5

stops.name: Garden House: death
stops.date_confidence: attested, 26 January 1895, at about six in the evening, in MacTutor, Britannica and the Mill Road Cemetery project, the last of which supplies the 8 January attack and the 21 January collapse. No modern diagnosis exists; the century's phrase 'internal malady' is descriptive, not clinical. The obituary quoted below is tagged as reconstruction: the original newspaper issue could not be traced and the page carrying it was 403-blocked to raw fetch.
stops.campa: He has been ill for three years, with attacks that put him in bed for weeks at a stretch and a condition the century can only call an internal malady. He has edited seven volumes of his collected papers and leaves six, and he has held the Sadleirian chair for thirty-two years. A severe attack comes on the eighth of January. From the twenty-first his strength goes. He dies at about six in the evening on the twenty-sixth, in the house at the bottom of Little St Mary's Lane, seventy-three years old.
stops.quote: he is likely to be best remembered as the creator of an entirely new branch of mathematics by his discovery of the Theory of Invariants
stops.quote_source: Cambridge Independent Press obituary of Arthur Cayley (1895), as quoted by the Mill Road Cemetery project. Tagged as reconstruction: the original newspaper issue was not traced and the page's raw bytes were 403-blocked, so the wording reaches this file only through a summarizing fetch.

stops.name: Cambridge University Press: Forsyth completes the thirteen volumes
stops.date_confidence: the completion of the edition in 1897 by Andrew Russell Forsyth, Cayley's successor in the Sadleirian chair, is attested in Wikipedia and Britannica. No month applies. The contents of Forsyth's biographical notice were read directly in the archive.org text of volume VIII.
stops.campa: Andrew Russell Forsyth, who has taken the Sadleirian chair, finishes the edition his predecessor began: six more quarto volumes, the last of them in 1897, nine hundred and sixty-seven papers in thirteen books. He writes the biographical notice himself and puts into it the things a colleague knows: the conveyancing footnote in Davidson's Precedents, a fellow-pupil's memory of a young man too modest to mention his wranglership, a correction of two anecdotes Cayley had denied in life. stops.name: Cayley crater, the Moon: the name goes off the earth
stops.date_confidence: attested in Wikipedia's article on the crater: formally named by the International Astronomical Union in 1935, with the name already circulating in nineteenth-century lunar nomenclature via William Radcliffe Birt and John Lee. No month applies. The coordinates are selenographic, not terrestrial: 4 deg 00' N, 15 deg 06' E on the Moon.
stops.campa: A crater on the southern edge of Mare Tranquillitatis, near four degrees north and fifteen east, has carried his name on lunar maps since the nineteenth century, put there by the selenographers William Radcliffe Birt and John Lee. In 1935 the International Astronomical Union regularizes lunar nomenclature and makes it official. It is a small flooded crater on a plain of smooth pale material, and the mappers name the plain after the crater: the Cayley Formation.

stops.name: Descartes Highlands: the Cayley Formation sampled
stops.date_confidence: attested in Wikipedia's article on Apollo 16: the site was selected on 3 June 1971 to test a volcanic-origin hypothesis for the Descartes and Cayley formations, and the returned samples disproved it, with House Rock delivering the final blow. Coordinates are selenographic, from the recorded landing site 8.97301 S, 15.50019 E. The first research pass called this 'four centuries removed' from Cayley; it is less than one.
stops.campa: On the third of June a NASA committee picks the Descartes Highlands for the fifth manned landing, because the smooth plains east of Cayley crater look volcanic on the photographs and nobody has brought back volcanic highland rock. In April 1972 two men land there, drive a rover across the Cayley Formation for three days, and hammer at a boulder they call House Rock. The hypothesis the site was chosen to test does not survive the rocks. The samples come home breccia; the plains are impact debris.

stops.campa: Sometime in the 1980s the stone goes. Local researchers cannot date the loss more closely than the decade, and what stands at the plot now is a broken stump. In 2021 a photograph turns up showing the stone still lying fallen at the site, so for some part of the interval it was face down in the grass rather than carted off. The grave of the man who gave matrices their algebra is a numbered plot with a stub of masonry on it, a mile and a half from a university that has a chair named for the woman whose bequest paid his salary.
